item.title: Trump called off Houthi strikes as military leaders debated risks of expanding war
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Donald Trump speaks in the Oval Office of the White House last week. (Samuel Corum / Bloomberg via Getty Images) WASHINGTON — U.S. military leaders are divided on whether President Donald Trump should get involved with the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, according to two U.S. officials. The Saudis have been asking Trump for the U.S. military to take action against the Houthis , a request that grew more urgent in recent days as the rebels claimed they shot down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet and were quickly advancing on Marib province, which is home to Yemen’s largest oil and gas fields. Some military leaders are making the case within the Pentagon and to Trump administration officials that opening another military front in the region is a bad idea amid concerns about the Pentagon’s dwindling supply of defensive and long-range weaponry, while noting that the Houthis are not striking U.S. ships, the U.S. officials said. Yet other military leaders are arguing in favor of strikes, saying the U.S. should help Riyadh retaliate for Houthi strikes in Saudi Arabia and the claim of downing of the F-15 — a challenge to Saudi air superiority over Yemen, the officials said. They said these military leaders are privately expressing concern that for the U.S. not to act more forcefully is a betrayal of an important regional ally. Trump had ordered strikes against the Houthis to begin around 5 p.m. Eastern Standard Time on Sunday, but the military was notified shortly after 2 p.m. on Sunday that the order was canceled, the two U.S. officials said. One of the officials said Trump has not taken military action off the table in the future. One senior U.S. military leader in the region specifically warned that action against the Houthis could create unmitigated risk to U.S. troops in Middle East and the Iran war mission, including a U.S. naval blockade and security operations in the Strait of Hormuz, the two U.S. officials said. They said the military leader also made clear that U.S. forces could carry out the Iran mission and strikes against the Houthis and mitigate some of the risks, the officials said. The internal divide underscores the bind the president is increasingly in as the U.S. remains locked in a war with Iran that he began but has struggled to end, and faces a shortage of key weaponry. The Saudis have been a critical U.S. ally in the Middle East, including throughout the war with Iran. Trump told Fox News over the weekend that he’s deciding whether to escalate the war with Iran, a position he has articulated on and off over the past few months. The White House and a spokesperson for the Saudi Embassy in Washington, D.C., did not respond to a request for comment. The Pentagon declined to comment. There has already been tension between the U.S. and its Middle East allies over the war. In May, Saudi Arabia was surprised by an announcement by Trump to help ships through the Strait of Hormuz and suspended the U.S. military’s ability to use its bases and airspace. Trump abruptly reversed his decision. The U.S. has already been supporting the Saudis by sharing intelligence, helping with planning, sending military advisers forward with the Saudi forces and even providing some logistical support, NBC News has reported. But the Saudis have repeatedly asked the U.S. to do more, including help with strikes against the Houthis. A satellite view shows the aftermath of the recent drone attack on the East-West pipeline in Saudi Arabia. The attack and the resulting fires, which occurred on Sept. 11, caused significant damage to the pumping station along the pipeline. (Vantor) Trump had not shown interest in acting until Thursday, when Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman told him in a phone call that the kingdom cannot succeed alone and after a series of developments — including the Houthis targeting Saudi infrastructure, downing the F-15 and threatening to take control of Yemen’s oil industry, according to one of the U.S. officials. After the call, Trump ordered the military to provide him with fresh options for strikes against the Houthis, the official said. Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Dan Caine called a 6 p.m. emergency meeting in The Tank, the top-security conference room in the Pentagon, to discuss options, the official said, canceling a trip to Copenhagen to meet with NATO chiefs of defense. U.S. military officials have presented Trump with options for degrading Houthi military capabilities and stopping the rebels’ recent advances several times since Thursday, the official said, adding that the Pentagon has enough assets in the region to be ready to act if ordered to do so. Saudi Arabia has closed the East-West pipeline while Houthi fighters captured key locations at the Bab el Mandeb strait (Javier Zarracina and Jiachuan Wu / NBC News / ISW; Natural Earth) The New York Times reported some details of Trump’s decision-making process. Violence escalated over the weekend , as the Houthis said they’d used missiles and drones on Saturday to attack “sensitive” sites in ‌Riyadh and an Aramco facility in the Red Sea city of Yanbu, a key oil export hub. The spokesperson for the coalition forces issued a statement on Saturday saying Saudi Arabia had successfully intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched toward Riyadh and that the Houthis “target civilians and civilian infrastructure in the capital.” The militant group also made a rapid advance to control the Bab el Mandeb Strait on the Red Sea, yet another oil chokepoint. The advance has posed a major challenge for the Saudis, who rely on that shipping route particularly since the Strait of Hormuz has been largely shuttered during the Iran war. The Houthis took control of Yemen in a bloody civil war in 2014 against a Saudi-backed coalition. A fragile truce between the Houthis and the Yemeni government backed by the U.N. was reached in 2022. Trump announced a ceasefire with the Houthis last year after weeks of punishing strikes against the militant group. Under the deal, the U.S. suspended military action and the Houthis stopped attacking U.S. ships. Trump recently has said his administration has had discussions with the Houthis but has not offered details. “The Houthis called us, and they don’t want to fight with us,” he said earlier this month. “They would much prefer not having us involved.” This article was originally published on NBCNews.com This article originally appeared on NBC News at https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/national-security/us-military-leaders-divided-action-houthis-rcna599049

item.title: He spent 11 months inside DOGE. Now he wants to set the record straight.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Tyler Hassen’s initiation into Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency, or DOGE, started as a series of tests. The Houston oil executive says he was given vague instructions to show up at an unfamiliar D.C. address. He hastily packed three suitcases and flew east, taking an Uber to a building that he soon learned belonged to Elon Musk’s SpaceX. He was whisked to a private office, acutely aware that his tailored suit stood out among the hoodie-clad engineers “too locked in” to their laptops to look up. He was ordered to go through the website of the Department of Commerce and, within days, find two to five ideas to present to Musk. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. He checked into a nearby J.W. Marriott and told his wife he didn’t know how long he would be gone. Thus began an 11-month stint at the center of a national firestorm - an exhilarating, chaotic and sometimes scary experience, Hassen told The Washington Post, in his first major interview detailing his forthcoming memoir and plans. The memoir, “Inside DOGE: The Real Story From a Senior Insider,” which recounts his time working for the secretive cost-cutting group, is the first tell-all to emerge from one of the most controversial periods of President Donald Trump’s time in office - a moment Hassen said he would gladly live through again. “There’s this misconception that we all just went in there and didn’t really think about what we were doing,” Hassen said, speaking virtually from a hotel room in San Diego. “I spent 24/7 thinking about it, waking up at 3 in the morning thinking, ‘Am I doing the right thing?’ … And I know I did.” At the heart of the book is a split screen: For many Americans, Musk’s project was a callous showcase of bending government to a billionaire’s will, associated with tens of thousands of federal layoffs, reams of lawsuits, an AI-enabled effort to kill off wasteful contracts and the gutting of the U.S. Agency for International Development. But Hassen’s memoir enters a different vision into the historical record: He portrays a period marked by a clash in worldviews, in which hardcore capitalists are granted unprecedented power to change a system that they argue operates under completely different incentives, logic and norms. To Hassen, whose pre-government career involved turning around distressed companies, “DOGE was not radical,” he writes in the book. It was “not a wrecking ball, but a catalyst.” In conversation, Hassen comes across as mild-mannered, a distant temperament from Musk, who famously brandished a red metallic chainsaw as a metaphor for cutting government waste. A 43-year-old dad with Boy Scout energy, he doesn’t cut the image of the nerd-engineer DOGE bro. He spent his entire adult life “hiring, firing, reorganizing and rescuing failing businesses” in industrial manufacturing and the energy sectors - a skill set that appealed to Musk, his longtime deputy, Steve Davis, and Baris Akis, a venture capitalist who served as a volunteer recruiter. But for years, Hassen seethed with rage over the national debt, now at $40 trillion. He felt angry that the amount the U.S. spends annually just to service that debt is more than the government spends on national defense and many other public benefits. So he raised his hand - making a cold outreach to Musk through a network of business world connections, he said in the interview, and pressed the point. “I’m staring at my daughter, who is 5, and thinking about her at 25 with $100 trillion of debt. And I know if we don’t do something about it now, we’re going to be there ,” he said . “ We’ve got to fix it now. ” By its own accounting, DOGE fell far short of the $2 trillion Musk claimed he would save, and an independent report from the Government Accountability Office has found DOGE’s own savings figures to be flawed. But Hassen told The Post he believes the effort was a success. “Did we eliminate the deficit? No. Of course not,” he said. “But we made it on the top of everyone’s minds, albeit briefly, for a few months, that this deficit is something that we need to fix.” In the book, he argues that “DOGE fit squarely” within a tradition practiced by some Democratic presidents, from Bill Clinton to Barack Obama, who also sought to shrink bloated government. DOGE was different, he goes on to concede, because of its speed, “faster than Washington was ready for and faster than its defenses could absorb.” But Hassen insists that DOGE was not cruel, a word that appears six times in the memoir, often in relation to laying off federal workers. The refrain can read as a plea for reconsideration of an effort he argues was poorly understood. “In the private sector, there’s an understood bargain,” he writes. “You’re hired to create value. If the value disappears, so does the job. It isn’t personal. It isn’t cruel. It’s the operating system of capitalism.” Government, he argues in the book, runs on a different logic. Value is “presumed,” “permanence is the default,” and “the moral burden of proofs falls on anyone who questions headcount - no matter how bloated the system becomes.” After the screening process, Musk and Davis deployed Hassen to the U.S. Department of the Interior, a sprawling agency that manages roughly 500 million acres of federal land and property, national parks, and tribal territories. He took the assignment, he wrote, because he knew “very little” about the agency and the challenge was appealing. Hassen was eventually promoted by Doug Burgum, the wealthy businessman who heads the agency, whom Hassen described as something of a kindred spirit. He became acting assistant secretary of policy, management and budget and stayed on until November - months after Musk himself had left Washington. During his tenure at DOGE, Hassen says, he put in 14-hour days, working nights and weekends. During the chaotic period he saw his then-4-year-old daughter only a handful of times. He said he relished the minutiae of the job: poring over grants written in what appeared to him to be bureaucratese, disassembling bloated org charts and consolidating departments. He says he encountered a bureaucracy more labyrinthine and redundant than he could have ever imagined. He caught spelling errors in a project description written by a vendor charging hundreds of millions of dollars, which he saw as proof of a systemic malaise. The contract, he writes, “stopped me cold.” (To drive home the point, a photo of the paperwork with the spelling error is published in the book.) He told The Post he was exhilarated to get deep into the bowels of the bureaucracy and deploy his corporate-honed skill sets to attack a problem that had long troubled him. During his first week at DOGE, the team met in a sparse conference room on the top floor of the SpaceX offices - empty except for a giant American flag on the wall, “because it reminded us why we are here,” he told The Post. “We had billionaires to 22-year-olds who had dropped out of Harvard, all sitting there on our laptops working with public information - trying to figure out how we can help solve this deficit, this crisis that we’re in.” As the group grew, the meetings moved to the Eisenhower Executive Office Building. There, he told The Post that he would present to Musk on a weekly basis, receiving the world’s richest man’s undivided attention. “He has this ability to grasp so many things, from California water to certain contracts,” he said. “We would talk about certain departments for 45 minutes - and how can we fix this - and we’d stay until 2 in the morning.” One time, after a particularly grueling session, Hassen said, he had to sneak out of the White House grounds to sleep. “I was so tired,” he said. During his time at Interior, Hassen was almost like a Where’s Waldo character, popping up at key moments that caught the country’s attention. When wildfires struck California, Hassen made an unusual decision to fly to the state to grill local officials about why the state’s largest water plant wasn’t running at full capacity. The image of him at the Jones Pumping Plant in California became one of the first posts from the DOGE X account identifying its members - prompting a flood of hateful messages and threats to Hassen and his family, he said. When Trump renamed the Gulf of Mexico, it fell to Hassen to officially register the rechristened Gulf of America in the Interior Department’s Geographic Names Information System - a move that then triggered a broader recognition of the name change on Google Maps and other online directories. Hassen says he felt the difference in mindset between the public and the private sector every day. “It showed up in the way career staff spoke about ‘the workforce’ as something apart - almost sacred,” he writes. “Until we can say out loud that government is a workforce like any other - noble in purpose, human in composition, and subject to reality like everything else - reform will look like cruelty before it looks like competence.” There is a clear cognitive dissonance between DOGE insiders like Hassen, who saw himself taking on a deeply patriotic project, and many Americans, who according to polls viewed DOGE disapprovingly. Not surprisingly, Hassen believes the media is one culprit - treating “every reduction as a moral offense” and framing DOGE leaders’ demands for accountability as a “cruelty experiment,” he writes. But in the book, Hassen also reflects on how DOGE’s failure to communicate hurt its reputation. Though DOGE was announced with great fanfare - and its website broadcast tallied savings - in practice the project was highly secretive, with DOGE members often showing up in agencies wielding great power before ever appearing on an org chart. In the six months before the ill-fated cost-cutting effort imploded, its staff gave just a handful of interviews. Two, including one with Hassen, were on Fox News, and he told The Post that he almost backed out. They were done, Hassen writes, only in response to prodding from then-White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt and Katie Miller, the political operative and podcaster who acted as a communications liaison for Musk’s effort. DOGE members were private citizens, fearful of being personally targeted and unfamiliar with the media apparatus that is part of Washington culture, he says. But fundamentally, the DOGE crew wanted to stay completely focused on the mission itself, he writes. The team was well aware that they needed to move with speed, as they might soon be slowed down by lawsuits, Congress or other bureaucratic forces. “We were there to work. We weren’t there to be public figures,” he said in the interview. In the book, Hassen implies that this was, to some degree, a miscalculation. “Once we stepped back, others were happy to define the work for us.” Ultimately, DOGE did lose control of the narrative, leading to a dramatic split between Trump and Musk five months after DOGE began and leaving the project in the lurch. The night of that split, Hassen said, he paced around the Interior Department like a ghost. The next morning, he went to the agency gift shop and bought his daughter a T-shirt that said “Future Secretary of the Interior.” He thought it might be his last night in D.C. Hassen’s experience working with AI for the first time at DOGE led him to take a new job leading Zone Frontier, a former cleaning supply firm with a new mission to provide infrastructure and permitting to the data center industry. Musk’s longtime lawyer, Alex Spiro, has also joined the board of directors, something Hassen said was a pure coincidence . He says he hopes the legacy of DOGE will be that the country’s most gifted citizens will seek to serve their government. Instead of draining the swamp, he says, he wants to flood it with talent and energy. “These are some of the best and brightest we have in America,” he said of the DOGE team. “I’m honored to be even a part of them.” Faiz Siddiqui contributed to this report. item.title: Iran threatens ‘new weapons’ as Trump weighs meeting with its president
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Iran warned Monday it would use “new weapons with new capabilities” if the U.S. launched a fresh assault after President Donald Trump ramped up the rhetoric against Tehran over the weekend. “If a new aggression takes place, we will definitely change the weapons and geography of the war,” Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesman for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said Monday, according to the semiofficial Fars news agency. Mohebbi did not provide details on what the new weapons were or which new locations could be hit. Earlier, Trump said he would “probably” be open to meeting with his Iranian counterpart, President Masoud Pezeshkian, during the United Nations General Assembly this week, Fox News chief foreign correspondent Trey Yingst reported Sunday. The possibility of a meeting offered a glimmer of hope for a resolution to the nearly seven-month war with Iran, which has resulted in Iran blocking the key Strait of Hormuz, and its Yemeni allies bombing a crucial east-west oil pipeline and threatening another crucial waterway. Resultant economic shock waves have hit the U.S. and the world economy, driving up oil and diesel prices and fueling inflation. President Masoud Pezeshkian stands beneath a giant portrait of Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei during a military parade in Tehran on Friday. (Morteza Nikoubazl / NurPhoto via Getty Images) Trump also said he was still deciding how to proceed with the war, describing his options as “wiping Iran out, letting them rot economically, or making a deal.” “My question is, if and when do I blow the entire nation up,” he said. “They better behave,” Trump warned. The president has previously said he did not believe the Iran war would end until after November’s midterm elections . He has also said oil prices would not come down until then. Oil prices slid to their lowest point in more than a week Monday as hopes for renewed talks between the U.S. and Iran grew, while signs of a recovery in Saudi crude exports eased supply concerns, despite continued attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis. Iranian students during an IRGC military parade in Tehran on Friday. (Morteza Nikoubazl / NurPhoto via Getty Images) Trump told Fox News that Washington was in constant communication with the Houthis — and that the Yemeni rebel group had agreed not to fight with the U.S., Yingst reported. Trump has said that the administration had been in touch with the Houthis, but did not say when. “The Houthis called us, and they don’t want to fight with us,” he said earlier this month. “They would much prefer not having us involved, and they’re letting most ships go through.” Violence escalated over the weekend, with the Houthis saying they had used missiles and drones to attack “sensitive” sites in ‌Riyadh on Saturday, as well as an Aramco facility in the Red Sea city of Yanbu, a key oil export hub. Meanwhile, fighting flared in southwest Yemen as the rebel group made gains against Saudi-backed forces. The New York Times reported Monday that the president had considered, but ultimately decided against on Sunday joining Saudi Arabia in joint strikes against the Houthis in Yemen. NBC News was not immediately able to independently confirm the newspaper’s reporting. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. “This is a really fluid situation,” Adam Baron, a fellow at the New America think tank who follows Yemen and the wider Gulf region, said Monday. He cautioned that he would not “rule out anything” when it comes to Trump’s stance on whether to help Saudi Arabia in its fight against the Houthis. Shipping data showed 17 commodity vessels passed through the Strait of Hormuz over the weekend, down from 37 a week earlier, though Middle Eastern producers continue to export oil on tankers with their transponders off, Reuters reported. A total of 22 tankers, mainly very large crude carriers, or VLCCs, exited Hormuz in the week of Sept. 13, with Saudi Arabia and Iraq each accounting for 43% of the volume, the outlet reported, citing data from tracking group Kpler, which maintains the MarineTraffic website. item.title: The 2026 midterms are 6 weeks away. What the latest polls say.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The 2026 midterm elections are just 43 days away. All of the key primaries have been decided . With summer officially behind us, the fall campaign is now underway. So where do things stand — nationwide — in the race to control Congress? Which party has a better chance of, you know, winning? To get a sense of that, it helps to zoom out … and geek out over some cold, hard data. The usual caveats apply, of course. Polls aren't predictions; they're momentary snapshots of public opinion. Big events can, and often do, change the course of elections. And six weeks can be an eternity in politics. Yet the stakes in November couldn't be higher, especially for President Trump, who has enjoyed complete Republican control of Congress for the first half of his second term. Flipping the House would give Democrats the power to block the president's agenda, investigate his administration and even impeach him (again); flipping the Senate would allow them to stymie his Supreme Court nominees too. The state-by-state midterm landscape is finally taking shape — and a few clear polling trends are emerging. Here are the numbers to watch as Election Day nears. The generic congressional ballot Every pollster asks a version of the same question: If an election for U.S. Congress were held today, which party's candidate would you vote for in your district? In fact, this particular polling prompt is so pervasive, it's known as the "generic ballot" (at least among politics nerds). You obviously can't divine the outcome of an entire midterm election from a single question that flattens 435 House contests into a binary choice between "the Democrat" and "the Republican." But the generic ballot can suggest which direction voters are heading. History is helpful here, courtesy of the RealClear Politics polling average : At this point in 2022 — after more than a year and a half of Democratic President Joe Biden and Democratic majorities in the House and Senate — Democrats had a narrow lead (1.3 percentage points) on the generic ballot. Six weeks later, the GOP translated its final polling lead of 3 percentage points into nine seats — enough to flip the House . At this point in 2018 — with Trump as president and Republican majorities in the House and Senate — Democrats were leading by an average of 8 points on the generic ballot. Six weeks later, they picked up 41 seats and flipped the House . Polarization wasn't as extreme in 2014 and 2010, the two midterms under Democratic President Barack Obama; minds weren't made up quite so early. But six weeks out, voters were starting to break against Democrats. In 2014, a final Republican polling lead of 2.4 points translated into a net gain of 13 seats in the House ; in 2010, those numbers were 9.4 points and 63 seats, respectively . So what does that mean for 2026? Historically speaking, a president's party almost always loses seats when voters return to the polls to judge his first two years in office. Sometimes, the backlash is so pervasive that the president's party loses pretty much every close-ish contest — a phenomenon known as a "wave" election. Right now, Democrats have a wave-sized lead on the generic ballot — about 8 percentage points , on average — and it has been steadily growing over the last two weeks. Democrats probably won't reprise 2018 and flip 41 House seats again in November, in part because red-state Republican lawmakers have recently redrawn congressional maps across the South to benefit their party in ways that blue-state Democrats have been unable to keep up with . But they only need to pick up three seats to win back the House. Advantage? Democrats. 10 specific Senate races National dynamics tend to define the composition of the incoming House. But Senate contests are quirkier — more state-specific and personality-driven. Democrats currently hold 47 Senate seats; they'd need 51 to control the chamber. (A 50-50 split would give Vice President JD Vance the tiebreaking vote). Polls suggest that flipping four Republican seats is possible — but Dems are also playing defense in places like Michigan, Georgia and New Hampshire. Here are the 10 races to follow: Maine (Republican seat) Republican Susan Collins (incumbent) Democrat Troy Jackson What the latest polls say : Jackson, who replaced Graham Platner , the Democrats' previous scandal-plagued nominee, tends to lead Collins by anywhere from 2 to 8 percentage points . One recent poll shows a tie . Michigan (Democratic seat) Republican Mike Rogers (former member of Congress) Democrat Abdul El-Sayed (public-health epidemiologist and former Wayne County, Mich. health director) What the latest polls say : Eight polls have been conducted over the last month. Seven of them showed El-Sayed in the lead, by anywhere from 2 to 5 percentage points . Ohio (Republican seat) Republican Jon Husted (incumbent) Democrat Sherrod Brown (former senator) What the latest polls say : Every poll conducted since July shows Brown leading Husted , with margins ranging from 4 to 8 percentage points. Georgia (Democratic seat) Democrat Jon Ossoff (incumbent) Republican Mike Collins (member of Congress) What the latest polls say : Ossoff holds a solid lead over Collins, with the two most recent polls putting him ahead by 4 to 7 percentage points . North Carolina (Republican seat) Republican Michael Whatley (former Republican National Committee chairman) Democrat Roy Cooper (former governor) What the latest polls say : Cooper leads by more than 8 points, on average . One poll conducted in Septemeber showed him ahead by 15 . New Hampshire (Democratic seat) Republican John E. Sununu (former U.S. senator) Democrat Chris Pappas (four-term U.S. representative) What the latest polls say: Pappas and Sununu, who both won their Sept. 8 primaries, have traded leads in recent polls in the race to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen. But the most recent survey, conducted from Sept. 16 to 17, showed Pappas ahead by 8 . Alaska (Republican seat) Republican Dan Sullivan (incumbent) Democrat Mary Peltola (former member of Congress) What the latest polls say : Most surveys conducted since Alaska's Aug. 18 primary have given Peltola a slim lead ; a mid-September AARP poll showed her ahead by 7. But the most recent sounding suggests this could be a photo finish. Iowa (Republican seat) Republican Ashley Hinson (member of Congress) Democrat Josh Turek (state legislator and former Paralympic athlete) What the latest polls say : Hinson and Turek have traded small leads in surveys released since Iowa's June 2 primaries . Texas (Republican seat) Republican Ken Paxton (state attorney general) Democrat James Talarico (state legislator) What the latest polls say : Nearly every poll conducted over the summer has shown Talarico leading Paxton, though the margins are small — between 1 and 6 points. Nebraska (Republican seat) Republican Pete Ricketts (incumbent and former governor) Independent Dan Osborn (veteran and former union leader with Democratic support) What the latest polls say : Surveys are few and far between. But the most recent results suggest Osborn could be competitive. Advantage? Too close to call — though Democrats seem to have gained ground over the last two weeks. Trump's approval rating — especially on affordability To one degree or another, midterm elections are always referendums on how the president is performing. So Trump is the final piece of the puzzle. At the moment, that's unfortunate news for Republicans on Capitol Hill and those looking to join them. According to the data journalists at Silver Bulletin , 59% of Americans, on average, currently disapprove of how Trump is handling his job vs. 39% who approve. That puts the president's net disapproval rating at 20%. An American Research Group poll released on Monday measured Trump's approval rating at 29% — his lowest mark ever. The same survey showed the president's disapproval rating at 68%. Again, history can provide perspective . In mid-September 2018, Trump was about 12 points "underwater"; Republicans went on to lose 41 seats that November. Trump is earning even lower marks on voters' top 2026 issue: the cost of living . Shortly after he returned to office, roughly equal numbers of Americans approved and disapproved of how the president was handling inflation. But today, 71% disapprove and 26% approve. That's a 45-point gap. In comparison, Biden's approval rating on inflation was rarely underwater by more than 30 points during his presidency — a period that coincided with the economic shocks of COVID-19 and ended with him choosing not to stand for reelection. Advantage? Democrats. Communities across the country are now pushing through moratoriums on new construction, often before developers can apply for permissions. Some 30 statehouses introduced or adopted rules pertaining to issues such as data center siting, electricity and water, the group said in a report Monday provided to Bloomberg News. The research quantifies growing concern about the rapid pace of expansion of artificial intelligence, both in the construction of new computing clusters and its proliferation into daily life. There are now 843 opposition groups across 49 states, with Hawaii the exception. “New groups continue to emerge, opposition is appearing across a wide range of states and jurisdictions, and online petition signatures continue to grow,” lead analyst Miquel Vila said. Data Center Watch is a project from AI intelligence company 10a Labs. Home to the biggest investors in AI infrastructure, the US is experiencing a bipartisan backlash against facilities that critics say harm the environment and siphon away resources in order to fuel AI systems that many fear will imperil jobs and livelihoods. Tech giants like Amazon.com Inc., Meta Platforms Inc., Microsoft Corp. and Alphabet Inc. — the so-called hyperscalers — argue they need the facilities to win a race against China to develop potentially world-changing AI. President Donald Trump has dismissed opposition to data centers and concern about advances in AI as a “sick conspiracy,” saying “the only one that is happy about it is China.” The number and value of disrupted projects fluctuates by quarter, with the first three months of this year seeing 75 cases worth roughly $130 billion facing opposition in the US. The 45 projects affected during the second quarter represented more than half of all new large-scale developments Data Center Watch began tracking during the period. Opposition by public figures and the use of social media are amplifying concerns. One petition against a project in Tennessee garnered over 500,000 signatures on online activism platform Change.org, accounting for more than one third of those on the service during the quarter, Data Center Watch said. For the first time since it began its research two years ago, Data Center Watch also reported on protests against data centers outside the US, given increased international opposition. Much as in the US, local campaigns are targeting specific projects, governments’ planning authorizations and worries about resource usage, sometimes coordinating nationally. item.title: 'Blatant violation' of rights: News outlets file lawsuit over Trump ban
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A growing list of news organizations has announced that they will not publish photographs from the White House on Monday in response to President Trump's move last week to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters from covering him or his administration in person. The Washington Post, the New York Times and HuffPost each announced Monday afternoon that they were joining the four major TV networks — ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox News — in refusing to participate in the White House pool, the rotating group of reporters, photographers and videographers that document the president's public events. As a result, Trump was largely inaudible during a ribbon-cutting ceremony for the White House's new helipad on Monday, where he gave a brief speech without the microphone that the pool would typically provide. Later in the day, the White House announced the creation of Trump TV , though details on what the service might include weren't provided. The three banned news organizations filed a lawsuit against Trump and three of his top advisers in federal court earlier Monday, demanding that access for their reporters be immediately restored. "This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes," CNN, MS NOW and Politico said in a joint statement. "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting. Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference." CNN had been scheduled to serve as the television pool on Monday. According to Politico , the four other major TV networks are declining to participate in White House pool duties moving forward in response to the ban. According to the complaint filed in U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C., the news outlets allege that Trump and the White House are retaliating against them for coverage they dislike. "President Trump has said in no uncertain terms that he would prefer only to be covered by news organizations and reporters who praise his administration," the complaint states. "But the Constitution does not allow a president or any other government official to deprive the press of their First Amendment rights and liberty and property interests with no notice or process based solely on his dislike of the content of their reporting." The organizations argue that their reporters were not afforded due process and are asking a federal judge to quickly rule that Trump's ban is unconstitutional. The filing cites a 1977 ruling by the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals, which found that the White House cannot arbitrarily deny a journalist a press pass without due process. "This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles," the filing states. Trump appeared to respond to the lawsuit in a social media post early Monday. "The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America," the president wrote on Truth Social . "It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!" The White House released a statement on Monday afternoon, saying that access for journalists is "a privilege — not a right." "The First Amendment protects their right to publish; it does not entitle them to a hard pass, briefing room seat, or place in the press pool," the statement read. "No President is required to host a hostile operation on the grounds. Access has always been a privilege — and President Trump is applying that rule." How the ban unfolded A view of the White House Briefing Room on Sept. 19. Graeme Sloan/Getty Images On Friday afternoon, Trump announced the ban in a Truth Social post , saying it was not prompted by any particular stories but was "a result of their constant 'reporting' FAKE NEWS!" "It's really just cumulative stories over the last few years. You get sick of it," Trump said at an Oval Office event an hour later while explaining his decision to enact "the ban on the free press." "There's something wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposely negative stories," the president said. "If they want to write them, that's fine, but I don't have to let them into my, into the people's house." According to CNN , Trump's close aide Natalie Harp showed him clips of media coverage shortly before he announced the ban. On Saturday, reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico were turned away from the White House by members of the Secret Service and had their credentials — so-called hard passes needed for access — confiscated. The journalists — CNN's Betsy Klein, MS NOW's Akayla Gardner and Politico's Cheyenne Haslett — are listed as plaintiffs in the court filing. MS NOW's Akayla Gardner, CNN's Betsy Klein and Politico's Cheyenne Haslett are seen near the White House after all were denied entry on Sept. 19. AP Photo/Jose Luis Magana The White House Correspondents' Association condemned the move, saying it violates the First Amendment. "The American people, through a free and independent press, must be able to scrutinize those elected to power, regardless of whether government officials view it favorably," Jacqui Heinrich, Fox News senior White House correspondent and WHCA president, said in a statement . "That's why courts have repeatedly held that once the White House provides access to journalists, it cannot deny that access arbitrarily or based on the content of their reporting." On Sunday, Trump posted what appeared to be an AI-generated image of trash bags bearing the logos of CNN, MSNBC (MS NOW's former name) and Politico outside the White House. The three news outlets are longstanding members of the White House press pool that provides rotating coverage of the administration and travels with the president. The daily guidance issued by the White House for Monday listed no primary TV pool, identifying Hearst and Real America's Voice as the "secondary" TV crews for the president's events in Washington and his scheduled trip to New York City for the United Nations General Assembly. Trump is scheduled to meet with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and French President Emmanuel Macron on Monday afternoon. The president vs. the press A White House staff member reaches for the microphone held by CNN's Jim Acosta as he questions President Trump during a news conference on Nov. 7, 2018. Jonathan Ernst/Reuters U.S. presidents throughout history have complained about negative coverage of their administrations. In 2009, the Obama administration sought to exclude Fox News from a series of interviews with a Treasury Department official in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis, but backed down when the other major television networks objected. Trump, however, has continued his adversarial relationship with the media, often referring to the press as the "enemy of the people." In 2018, Trump administration officials revoked the press pass of then-CNN White House correspondent Jim Acosta after they said that he had interrupted the president during a news conference. The network sued, and a federal judge ordered Acosta's credentials restored . A similar situation played out the following year when the White House revoked Playboy correspondent Brian Karem's press pass over a verbal argument between Karem and Sebastian Gorka, a former White House aide, at a Rose Garden event. A federal judge ordered the White House to restore Karem's pass . Last year, Trump barred Associated Press journalists from the Oval Office, Air Force One and some official events after the news service declined to refer to the Gulf of Mexico by Trump's preferred name, the Gulf of America. The AP filed suit and the case is ongoing. In his first event without a network TV pool on Monday, Trump unveiled the White House's new helipad before departing for New York. His remarks were nearly inaudible on the White House video feed . Joe Reberkenny, a White House correspondent for the Washington Blade who was serving as the in-town pool reporter, said he couldn't hear Trump "over the sound of the helicopter." item.title: Elon Musk's spending draws additional attention to Texas Senate race
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Musk has so far stayed out of the spotlight in the Senate race in Texas, even though he lives in the state, has based his companies Tesla and SpaceX there, and employs about 20,000 people. (Chip Somodevilla / Getty Images file) The last time Elon Musk sank money into an election, he played a starring role in the 2025 state Supreme Court race in Wisconsin. He donned an oversized cheese hat , offered $1 million checks to voters, and he and affiliated groups poured at least $20 million into the contest. In the end, the conservative candidate lost by 10 points in what was widely viewed as a rebuke of Musk and the Trump administration. Now, the richest person in the world is back boosting Republican candidates in critical midterm elections, including a bruising Senate race in Texas where Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton is facing Democrat James Talarico, who had initially far outraised him and remains close in polling. But that financial tide is quickly turning — with Musk’s help. Unlike in Wisconsin, Musk has so far stayed out of the spotlight in Texas, even though he lives in the state, has based his companies Tesla and SpaceX there, and employs about 20,000 people . He hasn’t announced plans for any in-person events, or teased — as he did in Wisconsin — that he’d be handing out $1 million checks to voters. Privately, Republicans say they want Musk to keep his distance. In interviews, more than half a dozen Republican strategists involved in the Texas Senate race say they hope Musk follows his 2024 model of electoral involvement, which led to a Republican sweep of the White House and Congress. Then, Musk spent more than $250 million on Donald Trump and his party. Republicans believe Democrats will attempt to turn Musk into a boogeyman if he takes on a higher-profile role in Texas or other battlegrounds. One Republican consultant involved in the Texas Senate race said that was the perception in Wisconsin. “He came in super late, and it was very public,” said the consultant, who, like others interviewed for this article, were granted anonymity to speak candidly. “Elon spending money became the story, which I think maybe was a mistake.” A different Republican strategist involved in Texas campaigns said those around Musk learned from the experience. “Did Elon bring some things to the Wisconsin race that hampered things? Probably,” the person added. “But I think they will adjust for that.” Democrats, however, say they welcome Musk more publicly entering the fray in Texas. “Elon, bring it. You’ve failed in Wisconsin. You’ll fail in Texas,” said Nathan Johnson, a Democrat running to replace Paxton as attorney general. “I’m not afraid of Elon bringing his political money here. All these policies favor him or people like him.” An in-your-face Musk campaign would play into Talarico’s narrative that the real American divide isn’t left versus right but “top versus bottom,” with elites and billionaires exerting control over the working class, they say. “James is running largely on costs and corruption,” Luke Warford, a Texas-based Democratic strategist and chair of the Travis County Democratic Party, said of Talarico. “The idea of the richest man in the world coming in late to try to buy the election and save Ken Paxton really plays into James Talarico’s argument.” The Texas Senate race has all the makings of a contest that would attract Musk. The conservative narrative building against Talarico amplifies his past remarks in support of transgender people, including his comment that “ God is nonbinary .” Talarico told Fox News he was being “provocative” and was trying to convey that one cannot use “human categories to define God.” Musk has spoken publicly about his own transgender daughter, Vivian Jenna Wilson, saying she was “not a girl” and was figuratively “dead.” He also alleged that he had been “tricked” into authorizing trans-related medical treatment for her when she was 16. Wilson previously told NBC News that Musk was an absent father who was cruel to her as a child for being queer and feminine. At this point, Musk’s America PAC has not said how much it will invest in Texas, but a person with knowledge of the group’s thinking indicated that as of now, the Paxton-Talarico contest was not slotted to receive more focus than other Senate or congressional races the group is investing in across the country, saying “every state and district where we are spending is a priority.” To date, America PAC has spent nearly $5.2 million on digital ads, mail, live calls and pamphleting in Texas, but that number is expected to significantly climb. In all, the super PAC has spent $14.7 million on congressional races, including seven Senate races and nearly three dozen House races. The group has spent the most money on the Texas Senate race, followed by nearly $3 million on Senate races in Ohio and Michigan. Trump boosted Paxton in the primary, even as much of the Republican establishment backed Cornyn. (Mark Felix / Bloomberg via Getty Images file) National Republican groups long knew they would have to provide air cover for Paxton because of an initial fundraising disadvantage to Talarico, who had $21 million in cash on hand compared to Paxton’s $1.7 million at the end of June, according to campaign finance reports. Today, a flood of Republican money is pouring in from several sources and the balance has suddenly tipped in Paxton’s favor. “America PAC is working in full coordination with the entire GOP apparatus and is investing in the states and districts that will decide control of the House and Senate,” America PAC spokesman Andrew Romeo said in a statement. “Our only priority is ensuring Republicans keep full control of Washington and stopping the lunatic left from bringing us back to the days of open borders, rampant crime, and woke policies.” Paxton’s status as a scandal-plagued candidate who has been impeached and indicted — coupled with the fact he’s coming off a contentious primary against Sen. John Cornyn and much of the Republican Party establishment, aside from Trump — makes him among the most vulnerable front-line Senate Republican candidates in a state where Democrats have not won a statewide post in three decades. After Trump’s late endorsement helped propel Paxton over Cornyn, groups like the Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC affiliated with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, and the National Republican Senatorial Committee, were left scrambling. The election cycle budgets were, in part, built on the idea that Cornyn would not need nearly as much national fundraising help. “Cornyn had his own fundraising machine, he could raise a lot of money on his own, so it was going to make things easier to cover other important close races,” said a Republican consultant familiar with the thought process. “I know they [Elon] are focused more on the ground game stuff. MAGA Inc. is on digital and mail. This pretty much turned out the way we thought it would. It’s an expensive endeavor and a team and multigroup effort.” Talarico had been raising significantly more money than Paxton. (Jordan Vonderhaar / Bloomberg via Getty Images) The pro-Paxton Lone Star Liberty PAC has pumped at least $15 million into TV ads that have included hitting Talarico on previous votes involving China. So far, MAGA Inc. has spent $10 million in the state to help boost Paxton, its second-biggest single-state investment. The group did not return a request for comment, but in an interview with NBC News last week, MAGA Inc. chief James Blair said the group had booked $10 million worth of TV ad time in Texas. Blair noted the previous disparity in spending, with Talarico and related groups pummeling Paxton on TV. “The fact is Ken Paxton had $100 million spent against him in the primary,” Blair said. “Talarico had $0 spent against him in the primary, and that has an impact on candidate images that takes time to rectify. But the resources … have begun to be deployed now in earnest [and] will take care of that problem.” A veteran GOP official directly involved in the race contended that the shift toward spending in Texas did not take away from other battlegrounds. “This spending will not take away from other investments,” the official said. “This came from a collection of Texas folks very committed to making sure that seat remains Republican. They see the polling, and that James Talarico is so extreme. No one wants to see Texas turn blue.” When asked about the onslaught of money headed toward Talarico, spokesman JT Ennis said, “Billionaire-backed dark money groups are lying about James because they’re scared of the people-powered movement we’re building to fix this broken, corrupt political system.” This article was originally published on NBCNews.com This article originally appeared on NBC News at https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-election/elon-musk-texas-senate-race-republicans-rcna596670

item.title: Man shot by ICE being detained with bullet still in his back, lawyer says
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A Venezuelan man who was shot by an immigration officer while delivering a DoorDash order in Austin, Texas, was transferred from the hospital to a detention center with a bullet still in his back, his lawyer said Monday. Wilber Rafael Garces Perez was shot in the back by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer after the officer sideswiped the 28-year-old's car early Sunday afternoon, attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch told reporters at a Monday news conference. Garces Perez was then taken to the hospital, and his family was notified four hours later that he had been taken to the South Texas Processing Center in Pearsall, Texas, approximately a two-hour drive away from Austin, Lincoln-Goldfinch said. Garces Perez spoke by phone during the news conference, saying in Spanish that he was in a lot of pain. He explained that the bullet wasn't removed because it was lodged close to his spine. "I am not doing well, and I am not receiving the medical attention that I require," Garces Perez said, adding that he's being held in a cold room with no bed. Lincoln-Goldfinch said her client also doesn't have access to pain medication at the detention center. Multiple law enforcement sources told CBS News the ICE officer who allegedly opened fire at Garces Perez has been placed on administrative leave, which is standard for officers involved in pending investigations. A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said in a statement late Sunday that Homeland Security Investigations, which is a part of ICE, is leading the investigation into the shooting with the assistance of the FBI. The spokesperson said Garces Perez illegally entered the United States under the Biden administration and had a final order of removal. "This is a developing situation, and we will update the public when more information becomes available," the spokesperson said. Garces Perez had a work permit and was seeking asylum, but he had received a deportation order in absentia after missing a court hearing because the notice was sent to his old address, his lawyer said. DHS has also terminated the parole status of those processed under the CBP One app last year and urged them to leave "immediately." In April , a federal judge in Boston ordered the Trump administration to restore their legal status, but DHS argued the president has the authority "to determine who remains in this country." item.title: Critics say California got too little in deal to let Paramount buy Warner Bros
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Jody Godoy and Chris Sanders WASHINGTON, Sept 21 (Reuters) - Critics swiftly decried a California-driven settlement with Paramount Skydance that cleared the way for its $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery, saying it will hurt competition in Hollywood, failed to protect jobs and lacks substantial ‌concessions from the media conglomerate. Opponents of the merger accused California Attorney General Rob Bonta and Governor Gavin Newsom of caving to wealthy interests, particularly ‌Paramount CEO David Ellison, after Paramount threatened to leave the state if the lawsuit was not dropped. "Today, billionaires have yet again bribed, censored, and bullied their way to the top," said Alvaro Bedoya, ​a former member of the US Federal Trade Commission and adviser at the American Economic Liberties Project. "Layoffs will follow. People from L.A. to Atlanta will lose their jobs, small businesses will lose their contracts, your cable bill and movie ticket will be even more expensive." Disappointment with the settlement rippled beyond Hollywood, illustrating a growing split in the Democratic Party between moderates, who are more business-friendly, and progressives, who seek a harder line to deliver affordability for US consumers. US Senator Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat from ‌Massachusetts, criticized the deal, and said Paramount is a "clear candidate ⁠for antitrust scrutiny in a future pro-competition administration." "This settlement greenlights an anti-monopoly disaster that will result in higher prices and fewer jobs, and enables a handful of billionaires to call the shots in the American media," she said. 'NOT A VOTE OF ⁠SUPPORT' Bonta, in a press conference on Monday, said the settlement is "not a vote of support" of the acquisition, because "it does not serve competition well." But he also argued it would amount to more production in California. Ellison said on Monday that the deal will strengthen competition and benefit consumers and workers. Spokespeople for Paramount and Bonta did not immediately respond to requests ​for ​comment on the reaction by critics of the deal. Bonta had said from the outset that ​structural remedies, where a company sells off part of its ‌business, are superior to promises to change or uphold business practices. Yet the settlement does not require Paramount to sell off any cable channels, or any component of what Bonta said made Paramount and Warner such a formidable combo in theatrical film distribution, such as its lucrative intellectual property. Paramount owns name-brand franchises including "Top Gun", "Mission: Impossible", and Star Trek, while Warner Bros holds the rights to Batman, Harry Potter, and "Lord of the Rings". The settlement includes the creation of independent editorial boards for CNN and CBS, and a $30 million penalty per film for any shortfall against Paramount's pledge to release 30 movies annually, as well as a commitment to bargain separately ‌with television distributors. The commitments are temporary, however, and expire within three to five years. Ensuring ​the merger would not harm the US entertainment industry by reducing the number of theatrical and ​television productions was a top priority for many after the lawsuit was filed ​in July. Consolidation as well as cheaper alternative production locations have led to job losses in Hollywood. John Bergmayer, legal director at ‌Public Knowledge, said the merger "leaves fewer studios competing for scripts ​and talent, gives one company greater power ​to dictate terms to distributors, and reduces streaming choices. Consumers will face higher prices, while writers and other creative workers will have fewer employers bidding for their work." Bonta's bid to block the deal had its detractors, too. Iowa and Montana asked the US Supreme Court to step in and ​block the case, in a bid to protect the ‌deal. Cinema United, a trade organization representing theater owners, had urged Bonta to discuss a settlement with Paramount, in hopes of avoiding further ​uncertainty and disruption in the industry. Cinemark, AMC and Regal are part of the group, which represents 30,000 US movie screens. (Reporting by Chris ​Sanders in Washington and Jody Godoy in Austin, Texas; Editing by Bill Berkrot) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://finance.yahoo.com/news/critics-california-got-too-little-212429667.html

item.title: Jobs that earn six figures without going to college — and why they are rare
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
As college costs and student debt have Americans doubting the value of higher education, there's growing interest in high-paying jobs that don't require a degree - and in public policy supporting training for them. But six-figure jobs that skip a bachelor's degree do require more than a high school diploma and remain rare, according to an analysis released Monday by Niche, a higher education platform. The highest salaries for workers without a bachelor's degree are typically in jobs gated by federal certification or specialized training, including commercial pilots, air traffic controllers, elevator installers and nuclear reactor operators, the study shows. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. The findings counter an emerging narrative about the prevalence of six-figure jobs in the skilled trades that don't require higher education. Politicians and business leaders have touted careers in electrical work, HVAC and plumbing earning more than $100,000, arguing that a four-year degree is unnecessary for financial security. While those jobs offer healthy salaries, research shows their median earnings are more modest than salaries for less common occupations that don't require a bachelor's degree. Source: Niche analysis of 2025 U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data Using data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, Niche economist Allison Shrivastava found that only 9.4 percent of occupations with a median wage of $100,000 or more don't require a bachelor's degree. Those occupations account for just 0.3 percent of 13.8 million annual openings projected across every occupation in which a bachelor's is not a prerequisite. There are four times as many openings that do not require a bachelor's degree, but the jobs generally pay less. On average, the median earnings for those occupations are around $45,000 a year, compared with $96,000 for job openings seeking people with a bachelor's degree, according to the analysis. "There's a little bit of romanticizing the trades," Shrivastava said. "There are some trade jobs that you can make six figures right out the gate, but they are more the exception than the rule." Sign up for our Paying for College 101 newsletter She said that doesn't discount the power vocational training has to lift people out of poverty and provide economic success. But those workers have less earning potential than people with a bachelor's degree, and can have a harder time finding work in other fields without additional training, Shrivastava said. A study published by the National Bureau of Economic Research found the college wage premium - the extra pay degree holders make compared to workers with only a high school diploma - doubles over a worker's lifetime, from 27 percent at age 25 to 60 percent at age 55. Workers with college degrees obtain jobs in professions with greater scope for on-the-job training and wage growth, according to the study. Zack Mabel, interim director of Georgetown University's Center on Education and the Workforce, said degree holders earning six figures are typically much younger than those without a college credential earning the same salaries. He said no-degree occupations that yield the highest salaries require considerable work experience and technical skills that come with years of training. A college degree is still valued in the labor market, Mabel said, and that is reflected in wage disparities. Forty percent of mid-career adults ages 35-44 with bachelor's degrees earned more than $100,000 annually in 2024, compared with 13 percent of high school graduates, according to research from the College Board. Higher-paying jobs are often accessible to workers without college credentials because of apprenticeships and union trade programs, but many of these workers achieve sustained wage growth by becoming entrepreneurs, said Mary Alice McCarthy, senior director of the Center on Education & Labor at New America, a Washington think tank. "Where we see tradespeople do really well … is when they're able to start their own businesses, start their own contracting firms," she said. "The real path to long-term prosperity does require that kind of evolution." McCarthy said the decline of labor unions in the trades since the 1970s has broadly eroded earning power. Many lucrative manufacturing jobs were also lost during the Great Recession and replaced with lower-paying service jobs. Even though workers without a bachelor's degree have far more job openings than degree holders, McCarthy said the quality of available jobs outside of the skilled trades has gotten worse with fewer benefits, stagnant wages and more precarity. To offer more pathways to higher-paying jobs, private sector and government employers have been ditching degree requirements. Governors in more than 30 states, including Maryland, Colorado and Pennsylvania, have committed to skills-based hiring by removing bachelor's degree requirements for public sector roles. Both the Trump and Biden administrations revised degree requirements on federal jobs. But those efforts are undermined by how hiring managers evaluate candidates, said Mabel at Georgetown. "There's still a very big disconnect between the momentum around removing degree requirements and what plays out when it comes to who gets hired," Mabel said. "Folks who are more credentialed are much more likely to ultimately be hired into those roles ." In a 2025 study, Harvard Business School and the Burning Glass Institute found that fewer than 1 in 700 new hires benefited from no-degree policies. They examined more than 11,000 job postings at U.S. firms from 2014 to 2023 and found that hiring of candidates without a college credential only increased by 3.5 percentage points. Mabel said skills-first hiring must be widely adopted to produce meaningful changes in the labor market. Workers are taking on the risk that while their first employer embraces what they have to offer without a college credential, the next one may not, he said. While a bachelor's degree improves the chances of reaching higher rungs on the income ladder, Mabel said the return on investment in higher education varies based on the field of study. Students at a crossroads in deciding whether to pursue a degree or a trade should know there is no one path to a lucrative job, said McCarthy at New America. And those positions require some form of education after high school, whether that means a certificate, associate's degree or bachelor's. Todd Wallack contributed to this report. - - - Graphics: Reality versus perception Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/articles/jobs-earn-six-figures-without-121553473.html

item.title: Vermont man convicted of attempted murder in shooting of 3 Palestinian college students
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Burlington, Vt. (AP) — A jury on Monday convicted a Vermont man of attempted murder in the shootings of three Palestinian college students who were walking near his home, rejecting an insanity defense rooted in his claims that he was acting on orders from U.S. and Israeli intelligence agencies. Jason Eaton faces up to life in prison in the November 2023 attack in Burlington, which paralyzed Hisham Awartani from the waist down and wounded his friends, Tahseen Aliahmad and Kinnan Abdalhamid. The men, all 20 at the time, had been visiting Awartani’s grandmother for Thanksgiving. They were smoking cigarettes and speaking a mix of English and Arabic as they walked near the University of Vermont campus after dusk. Two of them were wearing traditional Palestinian scarves known as keffiyehs. The jury deliberated for several hours before reaching its verdict after a weeklong trial that saw testimony from the three men, who recounted how their stroll ended in bloodshed, and defense and prosecution psychiatric experts who offered differing views of Eaton's mental health and criminal culpability. Eaton, 51, stared ahead blankly as the verdict was read, standing alongside his lawyers — public defenders whom he tried to fire last week over his concerns that his defense hadn’t been “adequately presented.” Judge John Pacht, who blocked Eaton’s midtrial bid to act as his own lawyer, ordered him jailed pending sentencing, which has yet to be scheduled. Awartani and Aliahmad watched from the front row of the courtroom gallery, smiling and hugging people around them. “The verdict cannot undo what happened or erase the trauma our families still carry, but it affirms something fundamental: Jason Eaton is responsible for what he did,” Awartani’s mother, Elizabeth Price, told reporters afterward. Eaton claimed he was acting on orders from the CIA and Mossad Eaton had pleaded not guilty but did not dispute that he was the shooter. He claimed that the CIA and Mossad transmitted their orders via FM radio and that God was commanding him to protect his Jewish neighbors. His lawyers had urged jurors to find him not guilty by reason of insanity, an outcome that would’ve spared him from prison but could have required that he undergo mental health treatment. Eaton's lawyers, Margaret Jansch and Joshua O’Hara, said he had struggled with mental health issues his whole life, including diagnoses of attention deficit, post-traumatic stress, bipolar, depression and borderline personality disorders, culminating in a psychotic break after losing his job at a credit union two weeks before the shooting. Prosecutor Sarah George countered that Eaton was a narcissist but not legally insane. He had a grandiose sense of self-importance and lacked empathy but was fully aware of the criminality of his conduct, George said in a closing argument. He appeared nervous when police arrived at his door, repeatedly asked for a lawyer and hasn't claimed to have received any other messages directing his actions, she said. Eaton told officers that he had a shotgun in his apartment, but didn't disclose that he had other weapons, including a Ruger .380-caliber handgun that was found in a bedroom dresser and that crime lab testing concluded was used in the shooting, said George, the Chittenden County state’s attorney. Victim’s mother says Eaton should’ve been charged with hate crimes The shooting, weeks after the start of the Israel-Hamas war, shook Burlington , and reverberated in the West Bank, where the three wounded men grew up and became friends as schoolmates in Ramallah before moving to the U.S. for college. It spawned calls for a hate crime investigation. But no hate crime charges were filed as questions persisted about whether anti-Palestinian animus, an altered mental state or something else had compelled Eaton to open fire. After the verdict, Awartani’s mother said Eaton's hateful rhetoric, aired at the trial, had made it clear why he targeted her son. Days after the shooting, George said in her closing argument, Eaton had told his lawyers that he wished Awartani’s grandmother had warned him that the men were “going to dress up like terrorists” and trek through his neighborhood. “Or see, if grandma had said to them, you know, maybe now’s not a great time to wear that thing on your head," George said, paraphrasing Eaton's remarks. “You know, things are a little tense when you’ve got American hostages over in Palestine, and we’re trying to get them back." “They were not the words of a man confused about who he shot or why,” Elizabeth Price said. “They were the words a man who saw three young men speaking the language of their childhood and wearing what made them feel closer to their far away families and homes and decided to kill them because of his own prejudices.” Victims recounted how a peaceful walk ended in bloodshed Awartani testified last week that he first noticed Eaton standing on a porch as they approached the apartment house where he lived. Within seconds, Awartani said, Eaton was off the porch and walking toward them. His face was expressionless and he didn’t say anything. As Eaton got to about 5 to 10 feet (1.5 to 3 meters) away, “he pulled out a handgun and started shooting at us,” Awartani said. Abdalhamid, a student at Haverford College near Philadelphia, said he fled and hid behind another home after seeing Aliahmad fall to the ground. He said he only realized later when he sat down that he had also been wounded. Awartani, who was studying at Brown University in Rhode Island at the time, was shot in the chest and the bullet ricocheted off his scapula, causing paraplegia in his spinal cord. Aliahmad, who was a student at Trinity College in Connecticut, was struck in the collarbone, and Abdalhamid was shot in the right buttock. Jacob Pyne, who lived in a different apartment in the same house as Eaton, testified that he heard four to six gunshots, followed by footsteps going up the stairs of the apartment house. He said he ran outside and heard two men speaking, one of whom was more vocal and yelling, “I’ve been shot, help me.” He then brought the men blankets and called 911. Eaton didn't testify. In an opening statement last week, O’Hara told jurors that Eaton claimed he started receiving messages while listening to a local NPR affiliate. At first, the messages were encouraging and validating, the lawyer said, but subsequent messages turned dark, insisting that Eaton “has to go out and shoot somebody.” This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/jury-convicts-vermont-man-attempted-173341045.html

item.title: Patrick Clancy opens up about forgiveness, grief and starting a new family
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Patrick Clancy spoke about coping with the deaths of his three children and how he has started rebuilding his life in his first televised interview since his ex-wife Lindsay Clancy's murder trial , The case has drawn widespread media attention, with the former labor and delivery nurse facing murder charges over the deaths of her three children — 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan — whom she admitted killing on Jan. 24, 2023. In an extensive interview with 60 Minutes aired on CBS News Sunday, Clancy said that at one point he "didn't think I would live to see my 35th birthday," as he struggled with grief. He said that he still dreams about his children, telling interviewer Ross Douthat, "it's like I'm lucid in those dreams." Clancy also discussed how he met his now-wife, Dr. Rachel Danis, who also appeared in the show, and said false online conspiracy theories about his involvement in his children's deaths were "deeply harmful to the legacy of my children." Clancy and Dr. Danis confirmed they are starting a family together. Here are the key moments from the interview. 1. He and his new wife are having a baby Asked by correspondent Ross Douthat whether the couple was "starting a family" together, Dr. Danis replied, "Yeah," with Clancy adding that he "can't wait" to tell any future children about their brothers and sister. "I think every parent can agree, you have different relationships with your kids, but they're all your kids," he said. "And I can't wait to tell them about their brothers and sister." On CBS Mornings on Monday, Douthat confirm that Dr. Danis was pregnant. "They are having a child," he said, acknowledging, "Maybe starting a family was too coy a way of asking it." 2. How Rachel Danis learned what had happened Dr. Danis, a fertility doctor, married Clancy in April this year. Joining her husband for the interview, she said that she first met him at a running club in New York in January 2024. She described finding out about his children while paying for coffee with Clancy during one of their meet-ups. "Pat pulled out his phone to pay, and I noticed this adorable photo of children as the wallpaper," she said. "And I just asked, 'Who are those cuties?' And Pat said, 'Those are my kids.' And then I think I asked if they live in Massachusetts, and Pat said, 'They died.' And this is just at the cashier." "I guess I had so many questions, and yet at the same time I didn't know exactly what to ask," she added. 3. He had a panic attack mid-testimony Clancy, who was the first witness to testify at his ex-wife's murder trial, told the court that when he returned from picking up food and prescriptions, he found his three children in the basement after calling 911 for Lindsay, who had jumped from a second-floor window. During the 60 Minutes special, he described having a panic attack mid-testimony and being put in an ambulance. "I went to a back room, and I started having this massive traumatic panic attack," he said. "My heart was pounding. And they put me in an ambulance. They offered me some medication, but I said, 'I — I don't want it, 'cause I want to go back and I want to finish this so I can be done with this.' And I went back and I finished the testimony." Recalling the 911 call being played in court, he said that "testifying is very difficult." "On the second day, a lot of that was focused on the night of January 24th. We did take a break right before they played the 911 call, which I knew was gonna be just horrific." The account rebuts what some online theorists interpreted as Clancy's stoicism on the stand, which in turn fueled conspiracy theories that he was somehow involved in the deaths of his children. These theories continued even after Clancy's lawyer warned he would take legal action against those responsible. Asked about the impact of the conspiracy theories circulating online , Clancy said, "It's painful to see. It makes it difficult to be in public, and it's possible that some of those people, after seeing lie after lie after lie, they start to believe it, and that's what we're left with." He said that the conspiracy theories are "deeply harmful to the legacy of my children." "It is a huge distraction from what really matters here, which is perinatal mental health. And it's done real harm to real people, myself included but also others," he added. 4. He didn't expect to survive his own grief — and forgave his ex-wife While Patrick and Lindsay Clancy are no longer married, Patrick Clancy told CBS he had forgiven his ex-wife for what happened to their children. Asked if she had ever asked for his forgiveness, Clancy said, "No. But I gave it to her." "I saw headlines that said, you know, 'Killer Mom,' and 'Baby Murderer,' 'Monster.' And none of 'em were accurate. I believe that it was her mental illness that caused that. So I shared those words. Lindsay Clancy has been held at a state-run hospital since 2023. Greg Derr/via AP "And I think when it comes to forgiveness, I also felt that if I didn't get there, I would be eaten up inside forever," he added. In the weeks following the tragedy, as Clancy tried to come to terms with life without his children, he discussed feeling so low that he had suicidal thoughts. "There was a time when I — I didn't think I would live to see my 35th birthday. And I was completely fine with it," he told the broadcaster. 5. Clancy's baby son died in his arms Two of the Clancys' children — Cora and Dawson — were declared dead on Jan. 24, but 8-month-old Callan remained alive for a few more days after being airlifted to Boston Children's Hospital. "I really thought there was a chance that Callan would live," he told 60 Minutes. "I remember just thinking, 'Just gimme one. Just gimme one kid,' and I would raise him as best I could, and I would give him the best life I possibly could. I'd tell him about his brother and sister. And I was holding out hope for that. "Then, when I got to the hospital, I saw the doctor. I saw the look on her face, and I knew that it wasn't going to be a good prognosis." During his final hours with Callan, Clancy said he sat and wrote tributes to each of his three children, typing with one hand while he held his baby's hand with the other. He told the program that he was afraid that if he didn't write about them, they would be forgotten. Callan's heart kept beating for four days before "he died in my arms," Clancy said. "I'm so grateful for those four days that I had with him. And I'm so grateful he hung on," he said. If you or someone you know is experiencing suicidal thoughts, call 911, or call the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-8255 or text HOME to the Crisis Text Line at 741741.
